title: KV segmentation map and prefetch controller for cross-parallel serving
creator: Alya Chen
description:
Problem: As context lengths and QPS grow, KV cache lookups and updates placed across tensor- and pipeline-parallel partitions become a dominant source of tail latency and GPU memory fragmentation. Continuous batching exposes non-uniform access patterns (prefix sharing + long-tail requests) that interact poorly with slab-only allocations and coarse static sharding.

Proposal: Introduce a KV segmentation map (logical segment-to-GPU mapping) plus an asynchronous prefetch controller to: 1) create fine-grained logical segments that can be moved/replicated independently, 2) track per-segment hotness and locality under tensor/pipeline parallel mixes, and 3) prefetch likely upcoming segments into local GPU memory using peer-to-peer when latency headroom allows. The prefetch controller is workload-aware (batch composition, recent KV hits, token position heuristics) and integrates with the continuous batching scheduler to avoid duplicative prefetches across in-flight batches.

Design highlights:
- Segmentation map: small (~4–32KB) logical segments derived from KV key ranges and stride-aware slicing. Segments map to primary GPU owners and optional transient replicas (ghost segments) for hot keys.
- Prefetch controller: asynchronous task queue per GPU that accepts predicted segment IDs, issues peer-to-peer transfers (NVLink/DC), and marks segments as "warming" in the local eviction/allocator. Prefetches are cancellable and reference-counted so multiple batches can reuse warmed segments.
- Eviction & consistency: owner GPU keeps canonical metadata; transient replicas use lightweight epoch-based validity tags. Eviction decisions combine LRU-ish hotness with pipeline-awareness (avoid evicting segments needed by downstream pipeline stages).
- API & telemetry: expose per-segment metrics (hit-rate, prefetch latency, replica count) in console; new rollout knobs for max transient replica memory and prefetch concurrency.

Why different from existing approaches: current slab/shard strategies assume mostly static ownership and large slab sizes. Segmentation map enables elastic placement and targeted prefetching, reducing both fragmentation and cross-GPU synchronization for long-context workloads.
acceptance_criteria: Linearized perf: tail P95 latency for generation workloads with 8k context reduces by >= 15% in mixed tensor/pipeline topologies (internal benchmark suite)
Memory overhead of transient replicas stays <= 7% of total KV memory in 99% of runs
Prefetch controller avoids >75% of inter-stage NVLink stalls observed in current baseline for hot prefix-heavy workloads
Design doc + implementation plan reviewed and approved by runtime and infra leads
Automated tests for segmentation mapping, prefetch cancelation, and epoch-based invalidation land and pass CI
Canary rollout on dedicated pool with controlled traffic and cost telemetry enabled
implementation_plan: Week 1: Prototype segmentation map and simple in-process prefetch queue (mocked peer transfers) to validate access patterns
Week 2–3: Integrate prefetch controller with allocator and implement transient replica allocation paths; add basic telemetry
Week 4: Implement peer-to-peer transfer paths with fallbacks (CPU staging) and refine cancelation semantics
Week 5: Run internal benchmarks across representative tensor/pipeline topologies and iterate eviction heuristic
Week 6: Add CI unit/integration tests and prepare canary rollout plan for dedicated cluster
Week 7: Design review and production canary; observe metrics and converge knobs for release
risk_and_tradeoffs: Memory vs latency: transient replicas reduce tail latency but increase peak memory; must tune replica budget carefully
Complexity: segmentation map and prefetch controller add coordination complexity between tensor and pipeline parallel components
Consistency window: epoch-based tags are eventually consistent; pathological traffic could cause brief stale reads unless owner fallback is fast
Hardware variance: performance depends on NVLink/PCIe topology; fallback paths for non-P2P setups will have higher latency
Testing surface: increases number of failure modes (mid-transfer cancels, owner GPU OOM, network interruptions) requiring thorough chaos testing
